data.text: Composing multiple HOCs lets you combine their powers into a single, enhanced component. However, understanding the **execution order** and knowing when to switch to hooks is critical for writing maintainable React code.

You can nest HOCs manually or use a `compose` utility. When HOCs are composed, they execute **from the inside out**. The innermost HOC wraps the component first, then the next HOC wraps that result, and so on.

data.text: When HOCs are composed, the order matters. The innermost HOC runs first and is closest to the original component. Use the table below to trace how props and behavior flow through a composed HOC chain.

data.title: Avoid Wrapper Hell
data.text: Composing too many HOCs creates deeply nested components that are hard to debug and style. If you find yourself wrapping a component more than 2-3 times, consider whether **custom hooks** or **component composition** might be a cleaner solution.

Modern React favors **custom hooks** over HOCs for most composition needs. Hooks let you extract and reuse stateful logic without changing your component hierarchy. However, HOCs are still useful for applying cross-cutting concerns declaratively.

cards.description: Wrap components with multiple HOCs to stack behaviors.
pros: Declarative - looks like a normal component in JSX
Easy to apply across many components

cards.title: Hooks Composition
cards.description: Call multiple custom hooks inside a single component to combine logic.
pros: Explicit data flow - see exactly what state is used
cons: Must call hooks at the top level
Cannot use hooks in loops or conditions

items.question: How many HOCs should I compose at once?
items.answer: Aim for 2 or fewer composed HOCs. Beyond that, you risk wrapper hell and difficulty understanding the component tree. If you need more, switch to custom hooks or break the UI into smaller components.

items.question: Do composed HOCs execute in parallel?
items.answer: No. HOCs execute sequentially. Each HOC wraps the result of the previous one. This means the first HOC in the composition chain is the innermost wrapper and executes first.

items.question: Should I always prefer hooks over HOCs?
items.answer: Not always. HOCs are still great for applying cross-cutting concerns like themes, authentication, or logging across many components. Use hooks when you need stateful logic inside a single component, and HOCs when you need to enhance many components uniformly.

items.question: Can HOCs access state from other HOCs in the chain?
items.answer: Only if that state is passed down as props. Each HOC in the chain is isolated. To share state between HOCs, pass it through props or lift the shared state to a parent or context.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: HOCs compose inside-out: the last HOC in code wraps first in execution
Use compose utilities for readable left-to-right composition
Hooks are preferred for most new React code
Avoid composing more than 2-3 HOCs on a single component
data.takeaway: Composition is powerful, but keep it simple with hooks when possible.

data.title: Compose 3 HOCs Around a Component
data.description: Take a simple `UserProfile` component and enhance it using three HOCs: `withAuth`, `withLoading`, and `withLogger`. Observe the execution order and verify that each HOC's behavior is applied correctly.
steps: Create a `UserProfile` component that accepts `user` and `onLogout` props
Apply `withLogger` to log every render of `UserProfile`
Apply `withLoading` to show a spinner while `isLoading` is true
Apply `withAuth` to redirect unauthenticated users to `/login`
Use manual nesting or the `compose` utility to combine all three HOCs
Verify the execution order by adding console logs to each HOC
data.expectedOutcome: A fully composed `UserProfile` component protected by auth, showing loading states, and logging renders.
